entries.title: AI risks can spread through the financial system
entries.summary: Federal Reserve Board — Governor Michael S. Barr, speech delivered November 16, 2026. Barr outlines potential risks from AI in financial markets and banking, including correlated trading, uncertainty about whether agents are authorized to act for customers, accelerated bank runs, and cyberattacks. These are risks for supervisors to monitor, not findings that these failures have occurred or binding new rules. The speech raises a systems question: safeguards for individual models may miss instability that emerges when many agents act together.
entries.question: How should supervisors test risks created by many AI agents acting at once, not just each agent in isolation?

sources.title: Some Potential Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence — Federal Reserve Board

entries.title: Can AI safety depend on trusting CEOs?
entries.summary: The Verge / Decoder — published November 14, 2026. CSET’s Helen Toner argues that AI safety should depend on accountable institutions rather than trust in individual executives. She discusses the tension between commercial incentives and safety commitments, and the role of technically informed policy research. These are an expert’s arguments, not new legal requirements or proof that every company’s governance fails. Why it matters: safety promises need practical authority to intervene. Reading angle: ask who receives evaluation results, who can delay deployment, and what happens when management disagrees. Policy term — institutional accountability: defined responsibilities, independent scrutiny, and consequences for organizational decisions.
entries.question: What powers would an AI safety board need for its ability to stop an unsafe deployment to remain credible under commercial pressure?

sources.title: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs

entries.title: What makes an AI safety evaluation credible?
entries.summary: Anthropic — published November 13, 2026. Anthropic’s guidance recommends involving subject-matter experts, designing tests around real use, measuring the intended risk, preregistering analysis, and documenting results. It is a developer’s methodology, not an independent certification or regulatory standard. Why it matters: deployment decisions can only rely on evaluations that test the right thing and make their limits visible. Policy term — construct validity: whether a test measures the concept it claims to measure.
entries.question: What evidence should an evaluator require before a higher safety score justifies giving an AI system more decision-making authority?

entries.title: A lawsuit asks a court to halt frontier AI development
entries.summary: Reuters — published November 12, 2026. Nonprofits sued several major AI developers and asked a California court to halt further frontier-model development under existing unfair-business-practices law. Claims of harm and the requested remedy are the plaintiffs’ allegations, not court findings or an ordered shutdown. Why it matters: the case tests whether existing legal tools can constrain frontier development without a new AI-specific statute.
entries.question: What evidence would justify a narrowly targeted development restriction, and how could a court decide when it should end?

sources.title: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic hit with lawsuit seeking halt to frontier AI development

entries.title: Companies turn to open-weight AI as costs rise
entries.summary: Reuters — published November 12, 2026. A Capgemini survey found that nearly six in ten large-enterprise executives plan to increase open-weight AI use as costs exceed expectations. These are reported intentions, not proof that the shift has already happened. Why it matters: organizations running models themselves also need to assign responsibility for safeguards, incident response, and later modifications.
entries.question: If a hospital runs an open-weight model locally, who should maintain safeguards and investigate failures?

sources.title: Most large firms plan higher open-weight AI use to cap bills, study shows

entries.title: Read first: Putting California’s frontier AI law into practice
entries.summary: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace — published November 10, 2026. This report examines how California can implement its existing SB 53 frontier-AI transparency law. It argues that developers can design risk-management practices, while public agencies need evidence and independent expertise to verify company claims. Recommendations address evaluations, incident reporting, and whistleblower protections; they are proposals for implementation, not newly enacted requirements. Why it matters: the central policy challenge is how to make verification credible while the technology and evidence keep changing.
entries.question: What information would regulators need to verify a company’s safety claims?

sources.title: Trust but Verify: Implementing Frontier AI Policy in California and Beyond

entries.title: Read first: Australia proposes mandatory AI safeguards
entries.summary: Prime Minister of Australia — published November 10, 2026. Australia announced plans for legislation requiring frontier AI companies to permit independent evaluations, rapidly report incidents, manage serious risks and publish safety frameworks. A proposed regulator would enforce these obligations with penalties; these are announced legislative plans, not already enacted requirements. Why it matters now: The announcement provides a concrete checklist for judging AI regulation: who must comply, what evidence they must supply, and who can enforce it. Watch the eventual bill for definitions, reporting deadlines and evaluator access. Policy term — incident reporting: a requirement to notify an oversight body when specified failures or dangerous events occur, enabling investigation and coordinated response.
entries.question: What evidence would convince you that human oversight is meaningful: a person approving outputs, documented overrides, or measured reductions in harm?

sources.title: New Australian AI safety and security protections

entries.title: Read first: Independence of government AI safety testing
entries.summary: Associated Press — published November 8, 2026. AP reports that U.S. government AI-safety staff were asked to report informally to a White House office, citing two former officials. Critics fear political interference; others see potential for greater influence and funding. This is reporting about oversight arrangements, not a new law. Why it matters now: Effective evaluation requires institutional independence as well as technical skill.
entries.question: What protections would let government AI evaluators publish uncomfortable findings while preserving legitimate security confidentiality?

sources.title: Staff at the US center for AI safety are reporting to the White House, raising independence concerns

entries.title: Read first: Singapore’s guidance on personal AI agents
entries.summary: CSA, GovTech and IMDA, Singapore — published November 6, 2026. Using Personal AI Agents Safely and Securely: What Consumers Should Know recommends narrow permissions, approval for consequential actions, and controls over retained personal information. Its key distinction is between instructing an agent to behave and restricting what its connected apps actually permit: users should not rely solely on chat instructions. This is government safety guidance, not a newly enacted AI law. Why it matters now: Agents can send messages, change files and expose information about people who never chose to use them. My policy takeaway: meaningful human control requires usable permission settings and activity records, not merely a warning that users remain responsible. For healthcare applications, this raises an especially concrete question about access to sensitive accounts. Policy term — least privilege: give a system only the access needed for its current task, limiting the damage if it makes a mistake or is manipulated.
entries.question: Which agent safeguards should be mandatory product defaults, and which can reasonably remain the user’s responsibility?

sources.title: Using Personal AI Agents Safely and Securely: What Consumers Should Know

entries.title: Read first: New federal DNA synthesis screening policy
entries.summary: NIH Office of Science Policy — published November 6, 2026. NIH explains a newly issued federal policy requiring recipients of federal life-sciences funding to purchase synthetic nucleic acids and benchtop synthesis equipment exclusively from verified suppliers that check customers and ordered sequences. Implementation is still underway: the existing 2024 framework remains applicable until the new policy is fully implemented. Why it matters now: For AI-biosecurity discussions, this illustrates an intervention at the physical supply chain: screening what researchers can order, alongside safeguards on what AI systems can explain or design. It also connects biotechnology governance directly to research funding and procurement. Policy term — nucleic acid synthesis screening: checking customers and requested DNA or RNA sequences before supplying manufactured genetic material, to identify potentially dangerous orders.
entries.question: How should policymakers divide responsibility between AI developers and DNA suppliers for preventing biological misuse without obstructing legitimate research?

sources.title: White House Issues New USG Policy for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening

entries.title: Read first: Independent assessment of AI research acceleration
entries.summary: METR — published November 5, 2026. After examining internal Anthropic data, METR estimates that capabilities on well-specified tasks are improving roughly twice as fast as during its earlier baseline period, with substantial uncertainty. It judges AI-assisted research likely responsible for most of that acceleration, but warns that Anthropic redacted much of the evidence most important to its conclusions. This is an evaluator’s assessment, not proof of an inevitable runaway intelligence explosion. Why it matters now: The report raises two linked governance questions: how quickly oversight must adapt, and whether an evaluation is publicly accountable when outsiders cannot inspect its strongest evidence. Policy term — independent evaluation: assessment by an organization outside the developer; independence alone does not guarantee unrestricted access or permission to publish findings.
entries.question: Should AI safety evaluators be guaranteed the right to publish evidence supporting their conclusions, and what narrowly defined exceptions should protect security or trade secrets?

sources.title: Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026

entries.title: Read first: How should the FDA regulate generative AI?
entries.summary: MedTech Dive — published November 3, 2026. The FDA is developing its approach to generative AI medical devices, and this article compares responses from industry, clinicians, patients, and researchers. Disagreements include whether existing oversight is sufficient, who should monitor deployed systems, and how evaluations should capture rare but serious failures. These are recommendations informing policy development, not newly enacted requirements. Why it matters now: This connects healthcare AI engineering directly to regulatory choices: strong average performance can conceal dangerous failures, and responsibility must remain clear after deployment. Policy term — postmarket monitoring: checking a product’s real-world safety and performance after it reaches users, so problems missed before release can be detected and addressed.
entries.question: If a healthcare AI passes initial testing but becomes unsafe during longer conversations, what evidence should regulators require before deployment—and who should be responsible for detecting failures afterward?
